title: Reading as a guest
hookLine: a sacred text belongs first to the people who pray it; read with that respect
tomorrow: why would anyone read the same three lines three times?

cards: At a friend's family wedding, the band plays a song half the room has streamed for the beat. Then the groom's grandmother starts crying at the second verse.
It was sung at her own wedding, in a language most of the room doesn't speak. Same song. The room knew the tune; she knows what it's for.

Year five opens old books, starting soon with the Dhammapada, and every one of them has a grandmother like that. So, one question for today: how do you read a book that belongs to someone else's family?

teach.b: This path has no scripture of its own. So every holy book it opens belongs first to the people who pray it, sing it, read it over their dead. That makes the reader here a guest.
And guests are an old subject.
In Genesis, Abraham sits at his tent door in the heat of the day, sees three men, and runs to meet them.
He bows and says, "Let a little water, I pray you, be fetched, and wash your feet, and rest yourselves under the tree." Then bread, and a meal. Later in the Torah, welcome becomes a command.
Leviticus says, "the stranger that dwelleth with you shall be unto you as one born among you, and thou shalt love him as thyself; for ye were strangers in the land of Egypt."

That's what this path shares with its Jewish neighbor: care for how guest and host treat each other. And the honest difference: in the Torah, the welcome is a commandment, with a people's memory behind it.

teach.h: A COMMAND THERE, A MANNER HERE.
teach.b: Here, reading as a guest is a manner you choose, and nothing commands it. What does the manner look like? A guest asks how the hosts read the book before deciding what a line means.
A guest says "Buddhists read this as", not "this really means". A guest never takes a line to use against the people it belongs to.
And a guest can be moved to tears and still be a guest.

how: Some readers outside a tradition start a sacred text by asking someone who prays it how their community reads it, and by reading a commentary from inside that tradition before forming their own view.

games.q: what does “reading as a guest” mean?
o: opening someone else's holy book with a guest's manners
borrowing a sacred book from a house of worship
reading only the parts of a book that agree with you

games.q: the guest and the host: tap the pairs.
p: asks how the hosts read it

s: once a holy book is for sale, any reading of it is as good as the next
the book belongs first to the people who pray it. a guest asks how they read it before deciding.
Leviticus tells Israel to love the stranger as themselves
and gives the reason: for ye were strangers in the land of Egypt.
reading as a guest means keeping your distance and never being moved
a guest can be moved to tears and still be a guest.

games.q: a coworker's family reads one psalm at every birthday. online you find a stranger's post on what it "really means". where do you start?
o: ask the coworker how their family reads it, then read it yourself.
the post; the writer clearly studied it, so it's the real meaning.
your own first impression; every reader's take counts the same.
games.why: a guest asks how the hosts read the book before deciding what a line means. the psalm is theirs first; your reading can come after.

practice: Take a pen and, by hand if you can, write one sentence: the manner you'll keep when you read someone else's holy book this year. It might be as short as "ask first" or "say whose it is".
Then sit with the sentence for the rest of the time and let it settle.

wordCard.voice: Reading as a guest: opening a holy book that belongs first to the people who pray it, and keeping a guest's manners at their table.

orig.note: Hebrew ger: the stranger who lives among you, the word behind "the stranger that dwelleth with you" in Leviticus 19:34.

carryVoice: For the road: as a guest, at someone else's table, with a guest's manners. Year five, begun.
